paper.title: LADDER: Self-Improving LLMs Through Recursive Problem Decomposition
paper.central_claim: LADDER: an LLM recursively generates easier variants of hard problems and trains itself with RL (GRPO) using a numerical verifier, improving Llama 3.2 3B from 1% to 82% on integration problems and Qwen2.5-7B-R1-distill to 73% on MIT Integration Bee 2025; TTRL (per-question RL on variants at test time) raises it to 90%.

evidence.quote: Second, we perform the reinforcement learning protocol
evidence.support_explanation: LADDER trains model weights on generated integral variants, rather than editing retained harness state.

evidence.quote: the model is rolled back to its original parameters for the next test question.
evidence.support_explanation: TTRL changes weights temporarily per problem; no cross-task harness persistence demonstrated.

evidence.quote: This transformation library served as a foundation for guiding variant generation.
evidence.support_explanation: Library is an initial generation aid, not an outcome-updated evaluated non-weight learning artifact.

evidence.quote: The problem is considered "solved" if the model produces a correct solution at any point during this process
evidence.support_explanation: TTRL outcome includes checker-selected attempts; scope decision does not depend on headline performance.

evidence.quote: LADDER achieved 82% accuracy on the test set
evidence.support_explanation: Reported improvement concerns the weight-trained solver.

evidence.quote: For our Llama experiments, approximately 8% of generated variants were effectively unsolvable
evidence.support_explanation: Generation failure is acknowledged; does not establish non-weight adaptation.

evidence.quote: While our current approach uses static parameters for variant generation
evidence.support_explanation: Adaptive generation-policy editing is future work, not current retained harness improvement.
Step 2 is RL (GRPO) on the base model over the variant trees; the output is a trained model, so the retained improvement lives in weights.

evidence.quote: We decided to employ Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) in both LADDER and TTRL
evidence.support_explanation: The improver acts through weight updates with a rule-based verifiable reward.

evidence.quote: The test question is then answered using the tuned model, and finally the model is rolled back to its original parameters for the next test question.
evidence.support_explanation: TTRL also modifies and discards weights per test question; no persisted non-weight component.

evidence.quote: approximately 8% of generated variants were effectively unsolvable
evidence.support_explanation: Variant generation (prompted transformation library, persona/temperature cycling) is a data-synthesis step feeding RL; its library is not evaluated as a retained artifact.

evidence.quote: We randomly split this collection into a training set of 10 problems and a test set of 100 problems.
evidence.support_explanation: Small design: 110 problems, 10 train roots, ~500 variants each, test 100; used here only to record the claim setting.

evidence.quote: We note, however, that the numerical verifier may not be 100% accurate.
evidence.support_explanation: Verifier admitted to be imperfect (random five-point numerical check).

evidence.quote: this comparison should be taken as a general baseline rather than a strict head-to-head evaluation
evidence.support_explanation: Authors qualify the o1 comparison (o1 has no numerical checker).

evidence.quote: and finally the model is rolled back to its original parameters for the next test question.
evidence.support_explanation: TTRL's adaptation is per-question weight training that is discarded; nothing non-weight is retained.

evidence.quote: This transformation library served as a foundation for guiding variant generation.
evidence.support_explanation: The only non-weight artifact is generated once by the base model and never updated from execution feedback.

evidence.quote: Second, we perform the reinforcement learning protocol described in section
evidence.support_explanation: Both LADDER and TTRL deliver their improvement through GRPO on model weights.

signatures.information: Training integrals, self-generated variant trees (depth<=3, 8% unsolvable), numerical verifier; test questions hidden except in TTRL
signatures.operation: Generate variant tree of easier problems -> GRPO with accuracy+format reward
signatures.selection_rule: reward 1/0; unsolvable/too-hard variants get zero reward
signatures.selection_data: variant trees from training roots (LADDER) or from the test question itself (TTRL)
signatures.failure_boundary: variants harder than parents; verifier imperfection; single domain

gap.author_gap: RL needs verifiable tasks forming a difficulty gradient; hard problems yield no signal and RL collapses.
gap.checked_gap: Gap is real for RL-on-weights; it is not a gap about a retained non-weight harness component.
lineage: STaR / self-play with interpreter verification (Haluptzok et al.) -> RL with verifiable rewards (DeepSeek-R1, o1) -> variant-driven curriculum (LADDER)
gap.closest_adjacent: Self-play puzzle generation and STaR as described in Related Work; no source texts fetched for them.
gap.residue: Unsolved hard questions give no reward.
gap.stakes: RL without variants stays <=3% then collapses to 0% (Llama 3B).
gap.method_response: Recursive simpler variants create stepping stones; TTRL repeats per test question.
gap.remaining_gap: Dynamic difficulty calibration, domains without verifiers, comparison with matched non-variant curricula.

claims.text: LADDER lifts Llama 3.2 3B from 1% to 82% on 100 held-out integrals and a 7B model to 73% on MIT Bee 2025; TTRL gives 90%.

claims.baseline_control: base pass@1/pass@10, RL on 10 roots without variants
claims.selection_vs_test: Train roots disjoint from test; TTRL uses test questions themselves
claims.result_denominator: 100 and 20 questions; MIT results averaged over 3 runs per text
claims.allowed_conclusion: Weights-level result; not assessed against the harness-level rubric.
